lead: The convolution integral gives the output of a continuous-time LTI system directly from its input and its impulse response. It adds shifted, scaled copies of the impulse response, one for every input value. Engineers use it to predict a circuit's response to a pulse, a loudspeaker's response to a click, and a communication channel's response to a symbol. The next step is to evaluate the integral reliably: flip the impulse response, shift it, multiply with the input, and integrate only over the overlap.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for LTI systems and Chapter 2.2 for the impulse response, plus Unit 1 for shifting and scaling of signals.

blocks.text: An LTI system is fully described by h(t), its output when the input is an impulse δ(t). Split any input x(t) into narrow pulses. A pulse of width Δτ at time τ has area x(τ)Δτ, so the system replies with x(τ)Δτ h(t−τ). Add all pulses and let Δτ→0. The sum becomes an integral.

blocks.where: t is the output time in seconds; τ is the dummy integration time in seconds; x(τ) is the input; h(t−τ) is the impulse response reversed and shifted by t; y(t) is the output.

blocks.text: The symbol * means convolution: y(t)=x(t)*h(t). The integral is also called the superposition integral. h(t−τ) is not h(τ). At a fixed output time t, h(t−τ) is h(τ) flipped left-to-right and moved right by t. The variable τ runs over the input's history.
For a causal system, h(t)=0 for t<0, so h(t−τ)=0 when τ>t; the upper limit becomes t. If x(t)=0 for t<0, the lower limit becomes 0. The algebra of convolution is in Chapter 2.4.
Graphical convolution is a five-step habit: sketch x(τ), sketch h(τ) and flip it, shift by t, multiply, integrate. It turns an abstract integral into areas you can see.

items: Sketch h(τ), then flip it to h(−τ).
Shift by t to get h(t−τ).
Multiply the two plots point by point.
Integrate the product only where both are nonzero: the overlap.

blocks.text: For finite-duration signals, the overlap changes at breakpoints. Write separate time cases for before, during and after the overlap. Do not use 0 to t blindly. In the example below, x lasts from 0 to 2 s, so the upper limit is t for 0≤t<2 s but stays at 2 s for t≥2 s.

A short numerical check uses the trapezoid rule. At t=1 s, y(1)=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup> e<sup>τ−1</sup> dτ. With step 0.5 s, sample f(τ)=e<sup>τ−1</sup> at τ=0, 0.5, 1 s: 0.3679, 0.6065, 1.0000. The trapezoid rule gives 0.5[0.5(0.3679+1.0000)+0.6065]=0.6452. The exact value is 0.6321. The 0.0131 difference is the rule's error; a smaller step reduces it. This check catches sign errors in the exponent.

figure.caption: The output rises while the shifted impulse response overlaps the 2 s input rectangle, peaks at t = 2 s, then decays. Notice that the decay after 2 s is not a new input, only reduced overlap.

spec.aria: Output rises to a peak near t=2 s and then decays, showing the overlap of a two-second rectangle with a decaying exponential.

examples.question: Let x(t)=u(t)−u(t−2) and h(t)=e<sup>−t</sup>u(t). Find y(t)=x(t)*h(t) for all t. Give y(1), y(2), y(3) to three decimal places.
steps: Write y(t)=∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup> x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ. Here x(τ)=1 for 0≤τ≤2 and 0 elsewhere; h(t−τ)=e<sup>−(t−τ)</sup> for t−τ≥0, that is τ≤t.
The product is nonzero only on 0≤τ≤2 and τ≤t. The overlap is 0≤τ≤min(2,t). This gives two time cases: 0≤t<2 and t≥2; for t<0, y(t)=0.

Case 0≤t<2 s: y(t)=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup> e<sup>−(t−τ)</sup>dτ = e<sup>−t</sup>∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup>e<sup>τ</sup>dτ = e<sup>−t</sup>(e<sup>t</sup>−1)=1−e<sup>−t</sup>. At t=1 s, y(1)=1−e<sup>−1</sup>=0.632.

Case t≥2: y(t)=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> e<sup>−(t−τ)</sup>dτ = e<sup>−t</sup>(e<sup>2</sup>−1)=e<sup>2−t</sup>−e<sup>−t</sup>. At t=2 s, y(2)=e<sup>0</sup>−e<sup>−2</sup>=1−0.135=0.865. At t=3 s, y(3)=e<sup>−1</sup>−e<sup>−3</sup>=0.368−0.050=0.318.
At t=2 s both cases give 0.865, so the pieces join. For t<0, y(t)=0.
examples.answer: y(t)=0 for t<0 s; y(t)=1−e<sup>−t</sup> for 0≤t<2 s; y(t)=e<sup>2−t</sup>−e<sup>−t</sup> for t≥2 s. The values are y(1 s)=0.632, y(2 s)=0.865, y(3 s)=0.318.
examples.check:
import math
y1 = 1 - math.exp(-1)
y2 = 1 - math.exp(-2)
y3 = math.exp(2-3) - math.exp(-3)
print(round(y1,3))
print(round(y2,3))
print(round(y3,3))

traps: The limits are the overlap of x(τ) and h(t−τ), not automatically 0 to t. For t≥2 in the example the upper limit stays at 2 s.
Flip h, not x, in y(t)=∫x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ. Flipping x gives a different integral.
h(t−τ)=e<sup>−(t−τ)</sup>, not e<sup>−t−τ</sup>. The shift changes the sign inside the exponent.
For finite-duration signals, split time at every breakpoint: before, during and after the overlap. Missing the t≥2 case loses half the answer.
Keep t and τ in the same time unit. A limit of 2 means 2 s only if t is in seconds.

quiz.q: State the convolution integral for a continuous-time LTI system and define each symbol.
quiz.a: y(t)=∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup> x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ. t is output time, τ is the dummy integration time, x is the input, h is the impulse response, and y is the output.

quiz.q: Why does a causal impulse response change the upper limit of the convolution integral to t?
quiz.a: For a causal system, h(t)=0 for t<0, so h(t−τ)=0 whenever τ>t. The integrand is zero above τ=t, so the upper limit becomes t.

quiz.q: Let x(t)=u(t)−u(t−1) and h(t)=e<sup>−t</sup>u(t). Find y(t) for 0≤t<1 and for t≥1.
quiz.a: For 0≤t<1: y=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup>e<sup>−(t−τ)</sup>dτ=1−e<sup>−t</sup>. At t=0.5 s, y=0.393. For t≥1: y=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup>e<sup>−(t−τ)</sup>dτ=e<sup>1−t</sup>−e<sup>−t</sup>. At t=1 s, y=0.632.

quiz.q: Let x(t)=1 for 0≤t≤2 and 0 elsewhere. Let h(t)=2 for 0≤t≤1 and 0 elsewhere. Find y(0.5), y(1.5) and y(3) in seconds.
quiz.a: Overlap length times height 2. For 0≤t<1, y=2t, so y(0.5)=1. For 1≤t<2, y=2, so y(1.5)=2. For 2≤t<3, y=2(3−t), so y(3)=0.

quiz.q: A student writes y(t)=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup>x(τ)h(t+τ)dτ. What is wrong and what should replace it?
quiz.a: The sign inside h is wrong; it must be h(t−τ), not h(t+τ). With causal h and x(t)=0 for t<0, the correct form is y(t)=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup>x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ.

quiz.q: For x(t)=u(t)−u(t−2) and h(t)=e<sup>−t</sup>u(t), explain why y(t) is not zero for t>2 s even though x(t)=0 there.
quiz.a: The system has memory. For t>2 s, h(t−τ) is still nonzero for 0≤τ≤2, so past input values still contribute. The output is e<sup>2−t</sup>−e<sup>−t</sup>, which decays but is not zero.

quiz.q: What is the dummy variable in the convolution integral and why is it called dummy?
quiz.a: The dummy variable is τ. It is called dummy because it is only an integration variable; after the integral is evaluated, τ disappears and the result depends on t.

beyond: Not for the exam. Convolution is how audio plug-ins add reverb: they convolve a dry sound with a room impulse response. Image blur is a 2-D convolution with a point-spread function. In communications, deconvolution tries to undo channel convolution, and FFT convolution computes long convolutions faster. Radar and ultrasound use convolution to model echoes. Search for 'convolution reverb', 'deconvolution channel equalization' and 'FFT convolution'.
